title: Eluned and the Missing Whisper
markdown:
The Rooftop Garden Conservatory took the afternoon in stripes. Sun laid gold across the basil. Spiderwebs wore the light like borrowed jewellery. Eluned Seals sat in her map-making nook behind the compost bin, compass open, parchment unrolled, whiskers carrying ink and the green smell of crushed mint. It was, she felt, a proper hour for charting.

She had promised Rosa the tortoise a survey by the eve of the Grand Summer Solstice: the garden as precise as a drawn grid. A large promise for a seal whose joy lived in measurements. Rosa, bless her unhurried shell, found stories in ferns that uncurled like questions and wisdom in a ladybird’s march. She felt the garden’s pulse. Eluned had decided, with ruler and patience, to catch that pulse on paper.

For weeks she had marked every petunia, every rogue sprig of mint, the prize pumpkins, the exact tilt of the sundial. She had even noted where the compost steamed on cool mornings. The map was nearly a masterpiece: neat, complete, and, she hoped, worthy of a friend who moved slowly enough to notice everything.

Then, that afternoon, a thumb-sized absence. The Zephyr’s Whisper — her miniature copper weather vane, so fine it could notice a cloud’s sigh — was gone. She turned the instrument tray twice. She checked the fold of the parchment. Without the Whisper, wind was a rumour. Her reputation as a surveyor felt suddenly as thin as old paper.

She scurried the nook. Watering can. Trowel. The grumpy snail’s terracotta pot. “Utterly gone,” she told the bumblebees, who had their own business.

Rosa, admiring a stubborn daisy, stretched her neck. “Eluned. Are you quite certain?”

“I have looked in all the sensible places. It has absconded.” Eluned’s flipper traced the map: every blade accounted for, and no whisper of air.

Rosa’s old eyes took their time. “Perhaps you are looking where you expect it to be.”

“It must be somewhere. A proper survey needs it.” The thought of an unfinished gift sat poorly. The sun leaned west. Shadows grew long fingers across the incomplete work.

She hesitated, then chose the less dignified courage: she would go on without the vane and let the garden argue. A bold plan, or a desperate one. On a rooftop, the difference is mostly posture.

The sunflowers came first, tall and neighbourly. Sunny, the cheerfullest, bowed a heavy head and delivered a pollen-filled hug. “Remarkable,” Eluned muttered, trying to look official while extracting herself from gold dust. She sneezed, which did not appear on any legend. She next gauged airflow with a spinach leaf, which seemed scientific until a gust claimed it and sent it to the next roof like a tiny flag of surrender. She watched it go, pencil poised, and wrote, a little helplessly, departed east.

She consulted the gnomes, who were rumoured to know things. Bartholomew, chipped of hat, pointed at the sky. “The wind remembers.” Gnorman, whose face had been surprised for years, giggled. “It tickles.” Amusing. Not, strictly, data. Eluned thanked them with the gravity she reserved for faulty compasses and moved on, flippers dusty with pollen she had not planned to collect.

The sky went rose and orange. A quieter fact arrived. She had been so busy asking how the wind blew — speed, direction, the missing copper proof — that she had not watched what it did. The sunflowers leaned together, a silent agreement. Living compasses. Rosa had as good as said so. Eluned had been staring at instruments and missing the stems.

Rosa ambled, shell a soft grey in the green. She paused at the lavender. “The scent is strongest when the air is still,” she murmured, “and it dances when it moves.” Eluned breathed. The garden offered a report no needle could write.

Then she stared at her own flipper. Not for work. For a glint.

The Zephyr’s Whisper sat there, snagged in damp fur, proud as a pin. It had caught during Sunny’s hug. She had hunted the whole roof for an absence that had been riding along, taking the tour.

Relief made her flippers foolish. Then a laugh arrived, the useful kind. She looked at the map — hurried notes of leans and lavender — and at Rosa examining a dewdrop as if dew were a kind of clock. The conservatory was not ending. Only the hunt was.

“Rosa,” Eluned said, spectacles adjusted, amusement still in her voice, “I must confess. The survey is not what I planned. The Whisper misplaced itself. Then it reappeared.” She held up the flipper. “It was here. The entire time.”

Rosa’s smile travelled slowly to her eyes. “And what did you discover about the winds while it rode with you?”

Eluned looked at the scribbles. No isobars. No tidy speeds. A record of how the garden answered air: the shared lean, the travelling scent, a leaf that had emigrated. She copied one last note in the margin — vane found on surveyor — and did not tidy it away.

She placed the little copper whisper on a stake by the basil, where the first stripes of sun had been. The vane trembled, doing the small work it had always done, now that she was looking. Then she set the parchment in Rosa’s patient feet. The solstice could have its grid. Rosa had a map of weather that had already happened, drawn by stems and noses, and a friend who had stopped hunting long enough to feel the air on her whiskers.
characters: Eluned (practical seal map maker), Rosa (tortoise friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
